Forefathers
fōr´fä-thẽrz
n. pl. (ancestors; those who went before in the line — rendering Greek progonoi and Hebrew abot rishonim)
From fore (before) and father. The Greek progonos means one born before; the Hebrew phrase is simply the former fathers.

Biblical Definition

Forefathers in Scripture is a two-edged word, and both edges are sharp. Paul can bless God for a line of godly ancestry: “I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience” (2Ti 1:3) — and in the same letter he names Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, so the blessing of a covenant household is fully acknowledged. But Jeremiah uses the same word for inherited apostasy: “They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, which refused to hear my words; and they went after other gods to serve them” (Jer 11:10). The Psalmist prays that the coming generation “might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God” (Psa 78:8). Peter is sharpest of all: the redeemed were bought “from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” (1Pe 1:18). So Scripture will neither despise ancestry nor sanctify it. What came down from the fathers must be tested by the word of God, and what fails that test is precisely what the blood of Christ redeems a man out of — including, and especially, the religion he inherited.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines forefather as an ancestor; one who precedes another in the line of genealogy, in any degree, but usually in a remote degree.

expand to see more

FOREFATHER, n. An ancestor; one who precedes another in the line of genealogy, in any degree, but usually in a remote degree.

2. In the plural, the progenitors of a family, tribe or nation, considered collectively.

TRADI'TION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity.

2. That which is handed down by tradition; and in the Scriptures often that which is vain and set against the commandment of God.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 1:3 — "I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day;"

Jeremiah 11:10 — "They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, which refused to hear my words; and they went after other gods to serve them: the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant which I made with their fathers."

1 Peter 1:18 — "Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers;"

Psalm 78:8 — "And might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation; a generation that set not their heart aright, and whose spirit was not stedfast with God."

Modern Corruption

Inheritance is made the standard, so that what the fathers did is treated as proof that it is right — or, at the other extreme, every inherited thing is discarded because it is inherited.

expand to see more

Rome builds a doctrine of tradition on the fathers, setting an unwritten deposit beside the Scriptures as a second authority. First Peter 1:18 stands squarely against it: what came by tradition from the fathers was the very vain conversation from which the blood of Christ redeemed them. Scripture honours faithful ancestry — Paul serves God from his forefathers, Timothy has an unfeigned faith that dwelt first in his grandmother — but the honour is given because their faith was true, not because it was old. Antiquity is not a warrant. Jeremiah's generation had the longest religious pedigree in the world and had inherited the iniquities with it.

The opposite error is now the more fashionable: to treat inheritance itself as a defect, and every practice received from the fathers as a limitation to be outgrown. Psalm 78 refutes this by its own structure. The Psalmist tells the coming generation the works of God precisely so that they might not be as their fathers, stubborn and rebellious — the remedy for a bad inheritance is a better one, faithfully handed on, not the abolition of handing on. A church that keeps nothing from its fathers has not escaped tradition; it has merely exchanged an old one for whatever the present decade supplies.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek progonos (G4269), an ancestor, forefather — 2 Timothy 1:3, 1 Timothy 5:4; Hebrew ab (H1), father, with rishon (H7223), former, first.

expand to see more

Greek progonos (G4269) — one born before, an ancestor; 2 Timothy 1:3 and 1 Timothy 5:4, of duty to parents.

Hebrew ab (H1) — father, in the immediate and the remote sense; the ordinary word for ancestor.

Hebrew rishon (H7223) — former, first, ancestral; joined with ab in Jeremiah 11:10.

Greek patroparadotos (G3970) — handed down from the fathers; 1 Peter 1:18, where what was handed down was vain.

Scripture praises and indicts ancestry with the same word, and the test in both cases is the word of God.

Usage

"“Whom I serve from my forefathers with pure conscience” — godly ancestry gratefully owned."

"“Turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers” — the other inheritance."

"“Redeemed… from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” — the blood buys men out of inherited religion."
